input.question: What happens if you freeze a super strong container full of water?
input.ground_truth: There are different types of “ice” depending on pressure. Typical ice is ice-I; when freezing water under sufficient pressure, different types all the way to ice-XVI have been produced, some are unstable and can’t be found in nature. Most of these are more dense than water (ie the water would shrink rather than expand). It is hypothesized that under sufficient pressure (e.g. a strong enough container shrinking in size) water would freeze into a metallic form of ice.

response.prediction:
Okay! Imagine you have a really, really strong box, and inside it, you put a lot of water. Now, if you put this box outside when it's super, super cold—like in the middle of winter, or in a freezer that's even colder than your home freezer—the water inside will start to get very, very cold.

When water gets really cold, it turns into ice! But here’s the thing: when water turns into ice, it gets bigger. It’s like if you have a cup of water and you put it in the freezer, the water grows and can break the cup if it’s not strong enough.

But your container is super strong! So, if it's strong enough, the ice will just stay inside and make the container feel heavy and cold. But if the container isn’t strong enough, or if the ice grows too much and pushes in the wrong places, the container might crack or break because the ice is trying to get bigger.

So, if you freeze a super strong container full of water, the water becomes ice and gets bigger. If the container is strong enough, it will hold the ice. If not, it might break!
